newsitem.title: USA: Lawrence Payton, one of The Four Tops, dies.
newsitem.headline: Lawrence Payton, one of The Four Tops, dies.

text.p: Singer Lawrence Payton, one of The Four Tops whose sweet harmonies included such 1960s-era hits as "I'll Be There" and "Baby I Need Your Loving," died on Friday, police said.
Payton, 59, died at his home in Southfield, Michigan, after a long illness, Southfield police said.
Payton was too ill to attend an April ceremony in California to install a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame with fellow group members Levi Stubbs, Renaldo "Obie" Benson and Abdul "Duke" Fakir.
Fakir told a Detroit radio station that Payton had recently been diagnosed with liver cancer, and passed away with his wife and family members at his bedside.
The four high school classmates from Detroit's North End neighbourhood first joined together in 1954 as The Aims, producing jazzy vocal harmonies in the style of the Four Freshmen and other groups.

Two years later, they changed their name to The Four Tops to avoid confusion with the Ames Brothers and recorded in various styles with several recording companies before Detroit's Motown Records, run by hit-maker Berry Gordy, signed them in 1963.

The label's songwriters Brian Holland, Lamont Dozier and Eddie Holland helped the group produce a string of chart-topping songs that included "I Can't Help Myself (Sugar-Pie, Honeybunch)," "Standing in the Shadows of Love" and "Bernadette."

Their success spread to England as one of Motown's most accessible "crossover" acts -- black performers whose love-centred lyrics were clearly enunciated and could be understood by whites. Matching zoot suits and slick choreography completed the act.
Beatles' manager Brian Epstein arranged a London concert for the group and a warm airport greeting from young, white English fans shocked the "four guys from the ghetto," Fakir later said.
In the 1970s, the group's hit parade waned and they left Motown, which shifted to Los Angeles, to sign with ABC-Dunhill and produced the hit songs "Ain't No Woman" and "Keeper of the Castle."

The group continued to perform into its fourth decade, but members slowed down to start families. Stubbs reignited some interest in the group when he performed as the basso voice of Audrey II, the man-eating plant in the movie "Little Shop of Horrors." The group also appeared in car and promotional advertising spots.
